$note: BroGram lessons. One lesson per CLO. No institution names, no pattern ids, no emoji.

lessons.title: One Table Won't Hold It
lessons.hook: Flat files fall apart the moment two facts need to change together.

blocks.heading: Why one giant spreadsheet breaks
blocks.body: Picture one giant spreadsheet holding every book and its author's name in every row. Rename an author and you have to fix every row they touch, or the data disagrees with itself. A database management system stores related facts in separate tables instead, then joins them back together for you. The relational model is this idea: split data into tables, one fact per row. Give each row a primary key, a value that identifies it and never repeats in that table. A foreign key sits in one table and points at another table's primary key, so the connection is stored once and checked, not copied everywhere.

steps.say: author_id is unique per row here, so no two authors can share one identity.
This foreign key points at authors, so every book must belong to a real one.
The author is stored once; books just reference it instead of repeating the name.
The join follows the foreign key back to authors to pull in the name.

blocks.prompt: A clinic keeps one flat sheet where every appointment row repeats the dentist's phone number. A dentist changes numbers and only this week's rows get edited. What is now true of that sheet?
options: The sheet holds two different numbers for one dentist and cannot say which is current.
The sheet rejects the edit, because a value repeated across rows can only change everywhere at once.
The older rows are now unreadable, since their number no longer matches the newer rows.
Nothing is wrong yet; a number only has to be correct on the most recent row.
why: Right — the same fact is stored many times, so a partial edit leaves the copies disagreeing.
A flat sheet enforces nothing; it holds whatever each row was last edited to.
Every row still reads fine on its own. The damage is that two of them now claim different things.
Every row is a live record, so an old row with a stale number is a wrong record, not an archive.
blocks.hint: Count how many places that one phone number lives once it is repeated on every row.
blocks.explain: A foreign key stores the dentist once and lets every appointment point at that one row, so a number change lands in a single place and no two rows can disagree.

blocks.prompt: This enrollments table already has a foreign key back to students. One line still repeats data live in place, so an update can drift out of sync. Find it.
blocks.hint: Look for a column that copies a fact the foreign key can already reach.
blocks.explain: student_name repeats data already reachable through the student_id foreign key, so a name change here won't match students and the two disagree.

bullets: A relational database splits facts into tables instead of one repeated sheet.
A primary key names a row; a foreign key points back to one.
Keeping a fact in one place stops updates from drifting out of sync.
blocks.remember: One fact, one place. The foreign key is the pointer, not a second copy.

blocks.say: Now go tell the difference yourself, one messy sheet and one clean schema at a time.

lessons.exitLine: Time to spot the real pattern in a real schema.

lessons.title: The Foreign Key's Address
lessons.hook: One line on the diagram decides which table needs the extra column.

blocks.heading: Where the foreign key lives
blocks.body: Look at an entity-relationship diagram and find the arrow between two boxes. One side is 'one', the other is 'many' — a coach has many teams, but each team has exactly one coach. That direction tells you exactly where the foreign key belongs: on the many side, pointing at the one side's primary key. Put coach_id on the teams table, never a list of team ids on the coach table. Relational columns hold one value each, so the side that would otherwise need a list is the side that gets the pointer instead. Every one-to-many relationship in a diagram follows this same rule: many holds the key, one gets pointed at.

blocks.caption: orders holds customer_id; customers holds nothing extra.

steps.say: authors gets a plain primary key because it's the 'one' side — nothing here needs to point anywhere.
books gets author_id because each book has exactly one author, but authors can have many books.
Two books reuse the same author_id, proving one author can back many rows without duplicating name data.

blocks.caption: One author, many books — the foreign key sits on books.

blocks.prompt: An employee works in exactly one department. A department has many employees. Which table should hold the foreign key?
options: both tables need a foreign key pointing at each other
neither table needs a foreign key
why: Right — employees is the many side, so it points at departments with department_id.
Departments is the one side; giving it employee_id would mean storing a list, which a column can't hold.
Only the many side needs a pointer; a two-way pointer just duplicates the same relationship twice.
Without a foreign key, nothing links an employee row back to its department at all.
blocks.hint: Find the side that would need to store more than one value if you got this backwards.
blocks.explain: employees is many, departments is one; department_id on employees points each row at exactly one parent without any list.

blocks.prompt: Finish the teams table so each team has exactly one coach, but a coach can run many teams.

tests.input: SELECT teams.name AS team, coaches.name AS coach FROM teams JOIN coaches ON teams.coach_id = coaches.id ORDER BY teams.id;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM teams WHERE coach_id = 1;

blocks.hint: The many side needs a column pointing at the one side's primary key — call it coach_id.
blocks.explain: coach_id on teams points at coaches.id; two teams can share a coach because a foreign key value is free to repeat on the many side.

bullets: The many side holds the foreign key, not the one side.
One-to-many never needs a list column, just one pointer per row.
A repeated foreign key value is normal — that's the 'many' showing up.
blocks.remember: Many holds the key, one gets pointed at.

blocks.say: Time to draw one yourself and turn it into tables that actually hold together.

lessons.exitLine: Draw the next diagram, then let the arrows tell you where every key goes.

lessons.title: Move it to where it belongs
lessons.hook: One column parked in the wrong table, and every edit means chasing down every copy.

blocks.heading: Ask what a column actually depends on
blocks.body: Every table should describe one kind of thing, keyed by one thing. If a column's value depends on only part of a multi-column key, or on some other ordinary column instead of the key, that fact gets copied onto every row sharing that value - and one edit can leave two rows disagreeing. First normal form breaks up a cell holding more than one value. Second normal form moves a column that depends on only part of the key into its own table, keyed by that part. Third normal form moves a column that depends on another ordinary column somewhere else. Each step removes one update anomaly: a fact stored twice that a single edit can leave disagreeing.

blocks.caption: Drill's name is typed twice. Rename it and you'd have to catch both rows.

steps.say: Every column above is supposed to depend on both parts of this key together.
Name and price only need product_id, so copying them per order risks two rows disagreeing.
Giving products its own key means a price fix lands in exactly one row.
order_lines keeps only facts about the order, linked back through product_id.

blocks.caption: One split, and the update problem disappears.

blocks.prompt: A table enrollments(student_id, course_id, student_email, grade) is keyed on (student_id, course_id). student_email only depends on student_id. Which fix removes the risk of two rows disagreeing about the same student's email?
options: Add a unique constraint on student_email.
Move student_email into a students table keyed on student_id alone.
Add student_email to the primary key alongside student_id and course_id.
why: Uniqueness stops duplicate emails, but the same email would still be retyped on every enrollment row.
Right. student_id alone identifies the student, so email belongs in its own table keyed on just that.
That makes the key even wider without fixing why the same email keeps getting copied per course.
blocks.hint: Ask what student_email is really about - a fact about the student, or about the enrollment?
blocks.explain: student_email depends only on student_id, not on course_id, so it is a partial dependency on part of the key. Moving it into a table keyed on student_id alone stores each student's email exactly once.

blocks.prompt: A table bookings(booking_id, room_id, room_type, nightly_rate, guest_name) is keyed on booking_id alone, but room_type and nightly_rate only depend on room_id. Write one query that returns the rows a separate rooms table should hold: one row per room_id, with columns room_id, room_type, nightly_rate, ordered by room_id ascending.
blocks.starterCode:
-- bookings(booking_id, room_id, room_type, nightly_rate, guest_name)
-- is already loaded when your query runs.
-- expected columns: room_id, room_type, nightly_rate

tests.name: two rooms, one booked twice
different rooms, still one row each

blocks.hint: Which two columns are duplicated across bookings that share the same room_id?
blocks.explain: room_type and nightly_rate depend only on room_id, not on booking_id, so distinct room_id, room_type, nightly_rate pulls out exactly the rows a rooms table should hold - one per room.

bullets: Ask what each column actually depends on, not just its table.
Move a column to the table its value truly belongs to.
Name it: each split removes one update anomaly.
blocks.remember: The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

blocks.say: New tables, new dependencies to hunt down - time to split one yourself.

lessons.exitLine: That's the split. Go find the next one.

lessons.title: Join Tables, Then Group Them
lessons.hook: JOIN plus GROUP BY is how two boring tables become one real answer.

blocks.heading: Join first, then group, then sort
blocks.body: A JOIN lines up rows from two tables using a shared key, so one row ends up carrying columns from both at once. Once matching rows sit side by side, GROUP BY can fold every row that shares one value into a single row, and an aggregate function like SUM or COUNT works out one number for each group. ORDER BY runs last, sorting those finished totals instead of the raw rows underneath them. That order is fixed: match rows first, fold them into groups second, sort the results third — never the other way around.

steps.say: JOIN lines up minutes with names first, so SUM only ever adds numbers that belong to the same member.
GROUP BY decides where one bucket ends and the next starts — one row in, one row out, per name.
ORDER BY sorts the finished totals, not the raw workout rows, so the biggest total lands on top.

blocks.caption: One join, one grouped sum, sorted so the biggest total lands first.

blocks.prompt: Same query shape, new numbers: Sam logs 10 and 15 minutes, Ravi logs 40. Sorted by total minutes descending, which name comes first?
options: Sam, because names sort alphabetically first.
Ravi, because 40 minutes beats Sam's combined 25.
Both tie, since only two rows are grouped.
why: Alphabetical order plays no part here; ORDER BY is sorting the summed total_minutes, not the name.
Right. GROUP BY adds Sam's rows to 25 total, and 40 beats that, so Ravi's row sorts first under DESC.
The totals differ, 25 versus 40, so nothing ties and one clearly outranks the other.
blocks.hint: Add up Sam's two rows before comparing them to Ravi's single row.
blocks.explain: GROUP BY first collapses Sam's two rows into one total of 25 and leaves Ravi's single row at 40; ORDER BY total_minutes DESC then puts the larger number, Ravi's 40, on top.

blocks.prompt: Two tables sit in front of you: games(id, title) and sales(id, game_id, copies). Write one query that joins them and returns each title with total_copies sold, highest total first.
blocks.starterCode:
-- games(id, title) and sales(id, game_id, copies) are already loaded.
-- return columns: title, total_copies (highest total first)

tests.name: one game sold twice
both games sold twice, order flips

blocks.referenceSolution:
SELECT games.title, SUM(sales.copies) AS total_copies
FROM games
JOIN sales ON sales.game_id = games.id
GROUP BY games.title
ORDER BY total_copies DESC;
blocks.hint: Join on game_id, group by title, then order the summed column, not the title, in descending order.
blocks.explain: JOIN pairs each sale with its book by book_id, GROUP BY title folds every matching sale into one row per book, SUM adds copies inside each group, and ORDER BY total_copies DESC puts the best seller on top.

bullets: JOIN matches rows across tables before anything else runs.
GROUP BY folds matching rows into one row per key.
ORDER BY sorts the finished totals, not the raw rows.
blocks.remember: Join first, then group, then sort — in that order, every time.

blocks.say: Time to write that join yourself, on data you haven't seen yet.

lessons.exitLine: That's the shape. Now go run it on a table you didn't build.

lessons.title: No Join, Just a Filter
lessons.hook: Forget joins - one document already has everything a match needs.

blocks.heading: A filter object plays the WHERE clause's role
blocks.body: You already know how a WHERE clause narrows down rows. MongoDB keeps records as documents inside a collection instead of rows inside a table, and a find() call plays the same role a WHERE clause did. You hand find() a filter: an object where each key is a field name and each value is what that field must match. Plain values mean equals; operators like $gt, $gte, $lt and $ne compare instead. MongoDB checks every document in the collection against the filter and hands back every one that matches, in the shape it was already stored - no rows to reassemble, because nothing was split apart in the first place.

steps.say: Each document already holds every fact about one order, so there is nothing left to join.
delivered: true keeps only documents where that field equals true, nothing else.
total: { $gt: 20 } compares instead of matching, so only bigger orders survive.
Both conditions sit in the same object, so a document must satisfy both to match.

blocks.prompt: A members collection stores { name, active, visits } per member. Which filter returns only members who are active and have logged more than 10 visits?
why: Right - active must equal true and visits must beat ten, both checked together.
$lt keeps visits under ten, the opposite of what the question asks for.
"true" as a string never matches the boolean true stored on active.
This only checks visits, so an inactive member with enough visits would still match.
blocks.hint: Look at what each key checks and whether both conditions actually appear in the filter.
blocks.explain: A filter object matches on every key inside it, so active: true and visits: { $gt: 10 } must both hold before a document counts.

blocks.prompt: This should return every non-VIP ticket priced under 50. It returns every non-VIP ticket instead, whatever the price. Which line is wrong?
blocks.hint: Count how many objects this call hands to find, then ask which one it actually filters on.
blocks.explain: find() filters on its first object only; anything in a second object is not a condition at all. Both keys belong in one object: { vip: false, price: { $lt: 50 } }.

bullets: A document holds every fact about one record already assembled.
find() takes a filter object matching field names to conditions.
Operators like $gt and $lt compare instead of an exact match.
blocks.remember: One filter object, checked against every document - no join required.

blocks.say: Time to write your own filters against a fresh collection, no examples to copy this time.

lessons.exitLine: Go run a real filter against a real collection.
